newsitem.title: USA: Clinton dodges questions on campaign contributions.
newsitem.headline: Clinton dodges questions on campaign contributions.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday dodged questions about whether the Democratic Party had received illegal foreign contributions as his campaign tried to create a sense that his re-election was inevitable.

During an appearance staged on a hotel parking lot to announce he had signed a minor bill into law, Clinton was asked repeatedly about charges leveled by House Speaker Newt Gingrich that Clinton is essentially "selling pieces of this country to foreigners" by accepting their contributions.
"It's election time," was Clinton's sole response as he walked away to prepare for his Wednesday night debate in San Diego against Republican challenger Bob Dole.

White House press secretary Mike McCurry and Clinton's campaign press secretary Joe Lockhart also dodged the substance of the allegations and instead attacked Gingrich for having ethical problems of his own.

"From our point of view, politically, the only thing better than having Newt Gingrich as Bob Dole's chief spokesman is to have Newt Gingrich speaking on ethics for Bob Dole. He's not credible," Lockhart said.
Gingrich is the subject of a probe by the House of Representatives ethics committee on charges he improperly used tax-exempt funds for political purposes.

Clinton, asked what he would do in the debate if Dole made a personal attack, said he would prefer to debate the issues. "The most important thing, I hope, is that it will be something people will feel better about when it's over."

Several Republican lawmakers on Sunday called for the appointment of an independent counsel to investigate whether the Democratic Party received illegal foreign contributions. This includes nearly $1 million from individuals tied to an Indonesian financial conglomerate, the Lippo Group.

Clinton's ties to Indonesian billionaire James Riady have been fiercely attacked by Republicans, who say the wealthy Indonesian has exerted influence over the president by contributing to his political causes and his inauguration.
Attention has focused particularly on John Huang, a former vice chairman of Lippo's California banking subsidiary who moved on to become vice finance chairman of the Democratic National Committee.

Newsweek magazine reports this week that Huang "has raised millions from Asian sources" for Clinton's re-election effort, including a gift of $425,000 from Arief Wiriandinata, the son- in-law of a major investor in Riady's Lippo Group.

The DNC was forced to return a $250,000 contribution solicited by Huang after checking into questions posed by the Los Angeles Times and finding the contribution came from a South Korean company. Vice President Al Gore said on Sunday it was not unusual for political parties to return contributions.
McCurry, in a heated exchange with reporters, denied the United States had altered its policy to help the company or had altered its policy toward Indonesia as a result of the campaign contributions.

Asked if there was the appearance of an ethical lapse, McCurry replied: "I think the appearance here is desperation politics on the part of those running against the president. They've got no other issues to raise so they are fanning the flames on this issue."

With three weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election, the Clinton campaign tried to convey a sense that Clinton was on the verge of a landslide victory. White House political affairs director Doug Sosnik said the campaign essentially agreed with a New York Times analysis that states with 325 electoral votes are leaning to Clinton, 101 are leaning to Dole and 112 are a tossup. It takes 270 for victory.

Sosnik scoffed at reports the Dole camp plans a major push for California and its 54 electoral votes, a state in which Clinton enjoys a lead. He suggested Dole was talking up California to ensure state Republicans are not angry at him while he is there during the debate this week.
"I think they want to make sure they get out of there alive with the locals," he said.
For his part, Clinton said he would welcome a fight for California "because I believe the people there are fundamentally fair-minded and forward-looking."
